<meta>continues from previous page: how they take notice of</meta> God, they warn us, and they command him to be worshipped everywhere. But the unlearned, and those of such a nature to whom fate did not truly proceed from the Lord to obtain gifts, nor even to have a notion of immortal Jupiter <note>Porphyry uses Jupiter as a name for the supreme God.</note> — not hearing the gods and divine men — rejected all the gods. Instead, they chose not only to follow the prohibited demons with no hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things alone by which God is adored. For God, as the father of all, lacks nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. Instruction purges, he says; imitation deifies the soul by working affection toward him. Indeed, he <note>Porphyry</note> preached God the Father well and said by what morals he must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, where the life of the saints is either praised or blamed. But among Christians there was only so much — or rather, he slanders as much as the demons wish, whom they consider gods. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in theaters and temples as service to the gods, and then to observe what is read, said, and heard in churches, or what is offered to the true God; from this one can understand where the building of morals is, and where the ruin. Who said this to him or inspired him, except a diabolical spirit? It is such a vain and fitting lie: that the Christians revere the demons, whose worship was forbidden to the Hebrews, rather than hating them. But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped — and whom we, as citizens in this mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love through the holy celestial angels and the powers of God, whom we call most blessed — forbids sacrifice to others. He thundered in the law he gave to his Hebrew people, and added a great threat, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made only to the worst demons and earthly spirits — whom he calls smallest or minor spirits — since in the Holy Scriptures these are also called gods, though not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations. The seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> clearly placed this in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Therefore, lest anyone think that sacrifice was forbidden to these demons but permitted to celestial ones, either all or some of them, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone." This means except to the Lord only. Perhaps someone might believe that he said "to the Lord alone" because he thought there is only one God to whom sacrifice should be made. This is easily found not to be the case in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> offers such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people. It was written in the Hebrew language, not obscure or unknown, but now spread abroad to all nations; in this law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in his law and his prophets? Indeed, one should not search, for they are not obscure or rare. Rather, one should collect the clear and frequent examples and place them in this discussion of mine, by which it appears clearer than light: that the true and supreme God wished sacrifice to be offered to none at all except himself. Behold this one thing, stated briefly, or rather grandly, threateningly, but truthfully by that God whom their most learned men proclaim so excellently. Let them hear, fear, and fulfill it, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follows. "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," he says, "except to the Lord only." Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us to be his. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord: You are my God, since you do not need my goods." The most excellent and best sacrifice to him is ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the victims which the Jews offered as a shadow of the future were to cease; and the Hebrew prophets announced through oracles that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to its setting, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine uses Porphyry's own praise of the Hebrew God to condemn the worship of multiple deities, citing the biblical prohibition against sacrificing to any but the Lord. He argues that true worship consists of moral imitation and the offering of oneself rather than external animal sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Hebrew Law, Sacrifice, Demonology, Septuagint, Psalms, Ethics, The City of God, Monotheism</keywords>
